title: The Civil Servants of Whitehall
text:
The British civil service is a strict hierarchy, with clear grades from top administrators down to clerical and office support staff. Everyone in it has a job, a salary and access to free health care. That made it an ideal place for the epidemiologist Michael Marmot to ask whether a person's rank by itself was linked to health.

An earlier study of male civil servants, begun in 1967, had already shown that men in the lowest grades died at far higher rates than those at the top. In 1985 Marmot and his team began Whitehall II, enrolling more than 10,000 men and women aged 35 to 55 who worked in twenty London offices. They recorded their health, habits and working conditions and followed them for years.

The first report in 1991 found a clear step-by-step gradient: the lower the grade, the worse people's health, from heart disease to self-rated health. Smoking, diet and other risk factors explained only part of it. Later papers from the same study, published in the 1990s, showed that having little control over one's own work was one of the strongest contributors to the higher rate of heart disease in lower grades.
lesson: Lack of control over one's own work is not just unpleasant, it can damage health. Leaders who share decisions and autonomy protect their people.
source: Marmot, M. G., Smith, G. D., Stansfeld, S., Patel, C., North, F., Head, J., White, I., Brunner, E., and Feeney, A. (1991). Health inequalities among British civil servants: The Whitehall II study. Lancet, 337(8754), 1387-1393.
